newsitem.title: UK: Iraq sugar imports seen slowing during US strikes.
newsitem.headline: Iraq sugar imports seen slowing during US strikes.

text.p: Sugar imports by private Iraqi traders are likely to be reduced during the U.S.-Iraq crisis but the commodity should still flow through Jordan and partially satisfy demand, sugar industry sources said on Tuesday.

The U.S. missile attacks on Iraq, which came after the U.N. announced a delay in the oil-for-food plan signed in May, would not dramatically affect the sugar flow into Iraq while Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba remained accessible, they said.
"It (the flow of sugar) is certainly going to slow a little bit as the Americans hit the Iraqis today," said one sugar broker with a European trade house.
"But the Iraqis have no other choice but to come through Aqaba," he said.
On Tuesday the Pentagon announced the U.S. military launched cruise missile strikes against air defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurdish groups.

While private traders have been importing mostly Brazilian sugar through Aqaba and also re-exports from Dubai's Jebel Ali refinery, no deal has yet been struck with any Iraqi state buyer since the oil-for-food pact was signed.
"The government will only buy through tenders and they haven't bought anything yet, they haven't tendered yet as the agreement has not been finalised," the broker said.
"It's bits here and there -- but there's no clear picture on the volume," he added.
Market talk has centred on an immediate Iraqi import requirement of as much as 100,000 tonnes of lesser-quality white sugar, to coincide with south Brazil's peak shipment period.
"I think there was a bit of hype about that (quantity)...but there may well have been many other commodities they needed with (higher) priority," said another sugar trader.

Since the U.N. imposed its Gulf War trade embargo on Iraq, it has been importing under 300,000 tonnes of sugar annually, mainly through Jordan and Turkey -- less than half its sugar needs before the 1991 war.
"Sugar has been going in through back doors anyway but it (the military action) is not going to make it any cheaper," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar.
But it remains difficult to gauge what is likely to happen to the sugar flow into Iraq as details of the trade into the country are sketchy at best.
"I would imagine the situation will remain blurred...but there may be some cutting back (temporarily)," he said.
"If it's just going to private merchants and then filtering out into areas of consumption...why should it stop?"
